Raven Chacon’s Echoes on Park Avenue
The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist on latest projects, art in NYC for Indigenous Peoples’ Day, and a Felix Gonzalez-Torres show misses the mark.

It’s a beautiful Monday to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, no matter what the federal government says. In a conversation with Associate Editor Phillip Pyle, Diné musician Raven Chacon discusses his recent improvised performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the “collision” at the heart of all music, and reclaiming the technologies of colonial violence through sound.

Read on for a guide to shows centering Native art around New York City — including Shelley Niro and Sarah Sense, two of my favorite artists — and a critique of a Felix Gonzalez-Torres exhibition that bizarrely glosses over the late artist’s AIDS advocacy and political spirit.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor
Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

links.text: Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

blocks.text: On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play. | Phillip Pyle
